newsitem.title: UK: Major tries to avert Euro defeat in parliament.
newsitem.headline: Major tries to avert Euro defeat in parliament.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major faced a possible parliamentary defeat on Monday in the first challenge to government unity since it lost its overall majority in the House of Commons.
A vote at 2200 GMT on the government's stance on the European Union's fishing policy will test the new parliamentary line-up before MPs begin a three-week Christmas break on Wednesday night.
A defeat would be embarrassing rather than fatal for the Conservatives, although it would be open to the opposition Labour Party to put down a confidence motion to be debated on Tuesday.
Labour's senior parliamentary business manager Donald Dewar has said he would only take this step if he thought he could win such a confidence vote.

Fisheries minister Tony Baldry declined to forecast a government win. "I think it is self-evident in the House of Commons now with very tight arithmetic that every vote is going to be very tight," he told BBC radio.

A group of Eurosceptic Conservatives and the nine-strong contingent of Ulster Unionist MPs will hold crucial meetings later in the day to decide how they should vote on the fisheries issue, a highly emotive subject for many MPs.
There were signs that both groups might be mollified.
The expected announcement of a further cull of cattle to combat mad-cow disease is expected to please the Unionists, Major's most likely prop now he has lost his parliamentary majority.

Any slip-up in parliament could force Major into an early general election. Last week a by-election left the Conservatives level in terms of seats -- 323 -- in the lower House of Commons with the combined forces of the opposition.

He has indicated that he has in mind an election on May 1, just three weeks before the last possible date. Major was defeated by two in an similar parliamentary vote on fishing a year ago. Since then his party's position in parliament has worsened because of defections and by-election losses.
The government is riven by divisions over Europe, and with his party over 20 points behind Tony Blair's Labour in the opinion polls, Major is desperate to avoid an early election.
Eurosceptic Conservatives say Europe's fishing policy is decimating the British industry and allowing foreign-owned boats to scoop up catches which should be theirs.
But Teddy Taylor, a member of the most recalcitrant anti-European faction in the party, indicated they might not stage a rebellion in Monday's vote.

"We have had some clear indications the government do accept that there is a real crisis facing the British fishing industry because of the (European Union), and that the government has got to do something about it," he said.

Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg could prove Major's salvation. He is expected to announce plans for the slaughter of 100,000 more cattle in a bid to get progress on lifting the export ban on British beef.
The Ulster Unionists are particularly keen on this idea as the grass-fed cattle herds of Northern Ireland would be likely to be the first freed to resume sales abroad.
But Ulster Unionist MP Martin Smyth denied it would sway himself and his colleagues. "We will be taking guidance tonight from...our fishermen who are across here today lobbying," he said.
